walkthroughs.body_html:
Transport in Plants — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Transport in Plants brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Transport in Plants.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

options: solute through membrane
water through partially permeable membrane
gases through walls
ions against a gradient
a concentration gradient
energy from respiration
a large surface area
a high pressure

mcqs.q: What distinguishes active transport from facilitated diffusion?
options: Active transport only happens in animals and facilitated diffusion only in plants.
Water moves towards the sugar because sugar attracts water molecules chemically.
Both move substances down a concentration gradient, but active transport is faster.
Active transport requires energy (ATP) and can move substances against the concentration gradient.

mcqs.q: In osmosis, which direction does water move?
options: Active transport only happens in animals and facilitated diffusion only in plants.
Water moves towards the sugar because sugar attracts water molecules chemically.
From a region of higher water potential (less concentrated solution) to lower water potential.
Water moves from high solute concentration to low solute concentration.

mcqs.q: What drives water up the xylem in a tall tree?
options: Capillary action alone is enough to lift water to the top of any tree.
Roots actively pump water up to the leaves like a heart.
Active transport only happens in animals and facilitated diffusion only in plants.
Transpiration pull — evaporation from leaves creates tension that pulls water up the continuous water column.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Osmosis”?
options: Smaller cells have larger SA:V ratio, making exchange more efficient.
Diffusion of water across a partially permeable membrane, from dilute to concentrated solution.
Alveoli, root hair cells, villi — adapted with large surface area and short diffusion distance.
Net movement of particles from high to low concentration; passive (no energy needed).

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Examples of exchange surfaces”?
options: Smaller cells have larger SA:V ratio, making exchange more efficient.
Alveoli, root hair cells, villi — adapted with large surface area and short diffusion distance.
Net movement of particles from high to low concentration; passive (no energy needed).
Difference in concentration of a substance between two regions.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Diffusion”?
options: Difference in concentration of a substance between two regions.
Net movement of particles from high to low concentration; passive (no energy needed).
Diffusion of water across a partially permeable membrane, from dilute to concentrated solution.
Smaller cells have larger SA:V ratio, making exchange more efficient.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Surface area to volume”?
options: Diffusion of water across a partially permeable membrane, from dilute to concentrated solution.
Net movement of particles from high to low concentration; passive (no energy needed).
Smaller cells have larger SA:V ratio, making exchange more efficient.
Movement against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Concentration gradient”?
options: Alveoli, root hair cells, villi — adapted with large surface area and short diffusion distance.
Smaller cells have larger SA:V ratio, making exchange more efficient.
Diffusion of water across a partially permeable membrane, from dilute to concentrated solution.
Difference in concentration of a substance between two regions.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Active transport”?
options: Alveoli, root hair cells, villi — adapted with large surface area and short diffusion distance.
Smaller cells have larger SA:V ratio, making exchange more efficient.
Diffusion of water across a partially permeable membrane, from dilute to concentrated solution.
Movement against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.

mcqs.q: A potato strip placed in pure water gains mass. If it was 5.0 g and is now 5.6 g, what's the percentage change?
A student measures water uptake by a leafy shoot using a potometer. Uptake increases on a warm, windy day. Which conclusion is supported?
options: Higher temperature and wind increase transpiration rate.
Transpiration stops in moving air.
Water moves down the xylem from leaves to roots.
Wind reduces evaporation from the leaves.

mcqs.q: Which tissue carries water and mineral ions from the roots up to the leaves?
options: Xylem
Phloem
Epidermis
Mesophyll

mcqs.q: A ring of bark (containing phloem) is removed from around a tree trunk. Sugars build up above the ring. What does this show about phloem?
options: Phloem transports sugars made in the leaves.
Phloem carries only water upwards.
Phloem carries mineral ions from the soil.
Phloem has no role in transport.

mcqs.q: Why does covering the lower surface of a leaf with petroleum jelly reduce transpiration more than covering the upper surface?
options: Most stomata are on the lower surface.
The upper surface has more stomata.
Water only evaporates from the upper surface.
The lower surface has a thicker waxy cuticle.

sequence.def: Absorb water from the soil by osmosis
Water crosses the root into xylem vessels
Water drawn up the stem in a continuous column
Water reaches leaf cells and evaporates
Water vapour diffuses out through open stomata
